OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $F(n)$ be maximal such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $F(n)$ vertices. Prove that $F(n)/\log n\to \infty$.
#82: [Er93,p.340][Er95][Er97d]
graph theory
Conjectured by Erdős, Fajtlowicz, and Stanton. It is known that $F(5)=3$ and $F(7)=4$. 
Ramsey's theorem implies that $F(n)\gg \log n$. Bollobás observed that $F(n)\ll n^{1/2+o(1)}$. Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov [AKS07] have improved this to $n^{1/2}(\log n)^{O(1)}$. Dyson and McKay [DyMc26] have improved this further to $F(n) \ll n^{1/2}$. 
In [Er93] Erdős asks whether, if $t(n)$ is the largest trivial (either empty or complete) subgraph which a graph on $n$ vertices must contain (so that $t(n) \gg \log n$ by Ramsey's theorem), then is it true that\[F(n)-t(n)\to \infty?\]Equivalently, and in analogue with the definition of Ramsey numbers, one can define $G(n)$ to be the minimal $m$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $n$ vertices. This problem can be rephrased as asking whether $G(n) \leq 2^{o(n)}$. 
Fajtlowicz, McColgan, Reid, and Staton [FMRS95] showed that $G(1)=1$, $G(2)=2$, $G(3)=5$, $G(4)=7$, and $G(5)\geq 12$. Boris Alexeev and Brendan McKay (see the comments and this site) have computed $G(5)=17$, $G(6)\geq 21$, and $G(7)\geq 29$. Dyson and McKay [DyMc26] have proved $G(7)\geq 30$, and $G(k)\geq \frac{9}{163}k^2$ for all large $k$.
See also [1031] for another question regarding induced regular subgraphs.
Additional thanks to: Boris Alexeev, Zach Hunter, Brendan McKay, and videlec

 Update (14 Aug 2026): Dyson and McKay have now proved G(k) ≥ (1/(2e)−o(1))k², equivalently F(n) ≤ (√(2e)+o(1))√n ([DyMc26] v3, arXiv:2604.08215), replacing the 9/163 recorded above.
My paper (arXiv:2608.08169 v2) concerns the opposite direction, which they deliberately left open. Write F(G) for the largest order of a regular induced subgraph of G, so F(n) = min of F(G) over graphs of order n. The conjecture: every graph drawn from a model in the type-based family defined in the paper satisfies F(G) ≥ (√(2e)−o(1))√n a.a.s. If true, √(2e) is optimal for that family, and any further improvement on the upper bound — in particular any counterexample to this problem's conjecture — must leave it. The family is narrower than "type-based" suggests; the paper says how narrow, and claims nothing beyond it.
What v2 proves: F(G) ≥ n^(1/2−ε) a.a.s., conditional on two hypotheses stated explicitly there. It also records a first-moment computation that independently identifies √(2e) (not a second proof), and 108 certified exact values of F consistent with the predicted crossover F ≍ min(n^(2/3), √(n/L)), L the least Lipschitz constant of the kernel. Data and an independent verifier: https://gist.github.com/arielelevy/c9cf5b142951db0c7d179a3656098835
Thanks to Dyson and McKay for their detailed comments on v1.

 Regarding Brendan McKay's question (06 Oct 2025) about testing single-vertex extensions quickly: here is a reduction that makes the test near-instant per graph, applied at the current frontier (order 29 → 30).
If $G$ has no regular induced subgraph of order $\geq 7$, then any such subgraph of $G+v$ must contain $v$. Writing $S = T \cup \{v\}$ with $|T| = 6$ and degree $d$, the conditions force every $u \in T$ to satisfy $\deg_T(u) + [u \in N] = d$, so $T$ is *dangerous* only if its induced degrees take at most two consecutive values $\{d-1, d\}$ — and in that case the only neighbourhood $N$ that creates a regular subgraph through $T$ satisfies $N \cap T = \{u : \deg_T(u) = d-1\}$ (with the extra requirement $|N \cap T| = d$). Each dangerous $T$ therefore contributes exactly one forbidden-pattern clause on $N$. Subgraphs of order $\geq 8$ are handled lazily (CEGAR): solve the SAT instance over the $|T|=6$ clauses, certify the candidate $N$ with an exact solver, and add any violated larger witness as a new clause. UNSAT is then a proof of non-extendability. A typical order-29 instance needs 5–10 lazy clauses and solves in seconds.
Applying this to graphs from the published sample 'regsub_ge7.29some.g6.gz': all 66 graphs tested so far are certifiably non-extendable to order 30. 
There is also a quantitative reason to expect this outcome for the entire sample. Each $|T|=6$ clause forbids a $2^{-6}$ fraction of the $2^{29}$ candidate neighbourhoods, so with $c$ clauses the expected number of surviving neighbourhoods is $2^{29}(1 - 2^{-6})^{c}$, which drops below $1$ at $c \approx 1276$. 
Across 10,000 graphs of the sample, the clause count is tightly concentrated: minimum 4,467, maximum 5,343 — between $3.5\times$ and $4\times$ the threshold, with not a single graph below it. So single-vertex extension of graphs with this profile is hopeless by constraint density, and (with the usual caveat that the sample is not the complete collection $R_{\geq 7}(29)$) the evidence points to $G(7) = 30$ exactly. Finding $G(7) \geq 31$, if true, would seem to require constructions that avoid this clause-density profile rather
than extensions of known witnesses.
Code and details: https://gist.github.com/arielelevy/0968dfbd5395921ea73a725259c3d36c
One detail worth recording: when the induced degrees of $T$ are all equal to $g$ there are two candidate values of $d$, namely $d = g$ (forcing $g = 0$) and $d = g+1$ (forcing $|T| = g+1$, i.e. the $K_6 \to K_7$ case) — a naive enumeration misses the second. 
Disclosure: this computation and the reduction were developed with substantial assistance from Claude (Anthropic). All SAT verdicts are exact and the certificates were verified independently.

 Combining the threshold values already listed gives a few further exact values of the function in the statement. Since\[
G(k)=\min\{m:F(m)\ge k\},
\qquad
F(n)=\max\{k:G(k)\le n\},
\]the results \(G(4)=7\), \(G(5)=17\), \(G(6)\ge 21\), and \(G(7)\ge 30\) imply\[
F(n)=4 \quad (7\le n\le16),
\]\[
F(n)=5 \quad (17\le n\le20),
\]and\[
5\le F(n)\le6 \quad (21\le n\le29).
\]In particular, \(F(16)=4\). These values and intervals may be worth recording in the main problem statement.

 Define $G(k)=\min\{ n : F(n)\ge k \}$, that is $G(k)$ is the smallest order on which every graph has a regular induced subgraph of order $k$ or greater. This is the same way Ramsey numbers are defined, and I find it easier on the brain. $G$ determines $F$ due to monotonicity.
In 1997, I computed G(2)=2, G(3)=5, G(4)=7, G(5)=17 but didn't publish it. I just repeated that computation now with fresh code and got the same result. The lexicographic product $P_4[P_4]$ is a short proof that $G(5)\ge 17$ but I don't know of a non-computational proof that $G(5)=17$.
Here are the counts, from 1 vertex to 16 vertices, of graphs which do not have a regular induced subgraph of order 5 or more: 1, 2, 4, 11, 31, 130, 728, 6027, 66308, 818276, 8336902, 45933753, 79888458, 23814804, 512906, 954.
I have examples to show that $G(6)\ge 19$ and $G(7)\ge 28$ and I'm still searching for larger examples. I don't know why there should be a small leap from $G(5)$ to $G(6)$ then a large leap from $G(6)$ to $G(7)$, but the fact that there are 8 regular graphs of order 6 compared to only 6 of order 7 might have something to do with it
My simple code for $G(5)$ took about 25 hours to show $G(5)=17$ but it cannot find $G(6)$ in a reasonable amount of time. I'm thinking about how to design a smarter algorithm. (Brendan McKay).

 here are some amusing weaker problems where I still do not a know how to get a $\omega(\log(n))$ lower bound.
1) let $\alpha(n)$ be the largest $k$ so that every $n$-vertex graph $G$ contains an induced subgraph $G'$ on at least $k$ vertices, so that all the degrees of $G'$ are equal mod 3 (the analogous problem mod 2 has a linear lower bound via a very slick old argument of Gallai, see also the semi-recent work of Ferber and Krivelevich (link) which shows that if $G$ has minimum degree then you can in fact find an induced subgraph of linear size with all degrees odd);
2) let $\beta(n)$ be the largest $k$ so that every $n$-vertex graph $G$ contains an induced subgraph $G'$, and a set $S\subset V(G')$ of size $k$, all having the same degree in $G'$.

 $\alpha(n)$ (and the higher order modular analogues) should all be linear I believe.
meanwhile, $\beta(n)$ has a $O(n/\log(n))$ bound. the construction is take one clique of size $n/\log(n)$, two cliques of size $n/2\log(n)$, 4 cliques of size $n/4\log(n)$, and so on. this was observed in this paper by Caro, Shapira, and Yuster; the same construction also appears in this paper of Noga, Michael, and Benny (where they study $F(n)$ and related problems).
I'm inclined to believe this upper bound for $\beta$ is also tight (though I am a little less confident, compared to $\alpha$).
